title: Accounting Changes & Error Corrections
description: Learn retrospective and prospective treatment of accounting changes and prior-period errors.
html:
Accounting Changes & Error Corrections

Financial statements sometimes need to reflect changes in accounting methods, revised estimates, changes in the reporting entity, or corrections of errors from prior periods.

1. Change in Accounting Principle

A change in accounting principle occurs when a company changes from one generally accepted accounting principle to another generally accepted accounting principle.

General treatment:

Apply the change retrospectively unless it is impracticable to determine the prior-period effects or specific accounting guidance requires another treatment.

Retrospective application means prior comparative financial statements are presented as though the new accounting principle had always been used.

The cumulative effect for periods before those presented is generally reflected as an adjustment to the opening balance of the affected component of equity, usually retained earnings.

Example

A company changes from one acceptable inventory accounting principle to another. If retrospective application is required and practicable, prior periods presented are adjusted to reflect the newly adopted principle.

2. Change in Accounting Estimate

Estimates are revised when new information or experience changes management's expectations.

Common examples include changes in:

  • Estimated useful life of depreciable assets
  • Estimated residual value
  • Expected credit losses
  • Warranty obligations
Treatment:

Changes in accounting estimates are generally accounted for prospectively.

That means previously issued financial statements are not revised. The new estimate affects the current period and, when applicable, future periods.

Example

Equipment originally had an estimated remaining useful life of eight years. New information indicates that it will instead last only five remaining years.

The company does not go back and recalculate depreciation for prior years. It uses the revised estimate prospectively.

Change in Estimate Effected by a Change in Accounting Principle

Sometimes a change in accounting principle is inseparable from a change in accounting estimate.

In that situation, the change is generally accounted for as a change in estimate and therefore applied prospectively.

Example

A change in depreciation method may reflect a change in the expected pattern in which an asset's economic benefits are consumed.

Because the effect of the change in principle cannot be separated from the change in estimate, the change is generally accounted for prospectively.

3. Change in Reporting Entity

A change in reporting entity changes the specific entities included in the financial statements.

When applicable, comparative financial statements are generally presented retrospectively as though the new reporting entity had existed during the prior periods presented.

4. Error Corrections

An accounting error is different from a change in estimate.

Errors may result from:

  • Mathematical mistakes
  • Incorrect application of accounting principles
  • Oversights
  • Misuse of information that was available when the financial statements were prepared
Prior-period errors:

Material errors in previously issued financial statements generally require correction of prior-period financial information rather than being treated as a current-period operating item.

When comparative financial statements are presented, prior periods affected by a material error are generally restated to correct the error.

If the error occurred before the earliest period presented, the cumulative effect is generally reflected in the opening balances of affected assets, liabilities, and equity accounts, including retained earnings when applicable.

5. Estimate Change vs. Error

This distinction is especially important on the CPA Exam.

New information changes useful life Estimate Change
Prior depreciation calculation used the wrong asset cost Error
New collection experience changes expected credit losses Estimate Change
Transaction was accidentally omitted last year Error

CPA Exam Memory Rule

Principle → Usually Retrospective Estimate → Prospective Reporting Entity → Retrospective Error → Correct Prior Periods

Key Takeaways

  • Changes in accounting principle are generally applied retrospectively.
  • Changes in estimates are generally applied prospectively.
  • Changes in reporting entity generally require retrospective presentation.
  • Material prior-period errors require correction rather than prospective accounting.
  • New information normally indicates an estimate change; misuse or omission of information already available may indicate an error.

quiz.prompt: A company revises the estimated useful life of equipment because of new information. How should the change generally be accounted for?

choices.text: Directly through accumulated other comprehensive income

quiz.explanation: A revision resulting from new information is a change in accounting estimate and is generally accounted for prospectively.
